title: The 2026 Berggruen Prize Essay Competition Topic: ‘A New Axial Age?’ | NOEMA
gist: Noema Magazine announces the 2026 Berggruen Prize Essay Competition on the theme 'A New Axial Age?', framing today's convergence of genetic engineering, AI and climate crisis as a possible civilizational hinge point akin to Karl Jaspers's original Axial Age, and lays out a $50,000 prize with strict rules on generative-AI use in submissions.

insights.claim: Noema previously published an essay by Otto Scharmer titled 'We May Be Entering A Second Axial Age,' proposing that humanity may be undergoing a transformation of consciousness comparable to the original Axial Age.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Signals that elite intellectual and philanthropic circles (Berggruen Institute) are actively promoting a 'civilizational inflection point' narrative tied to AI and biotech, which can shape policy and cultural framing around these technologies.
insights.locator: It follows an essay in Noema by Otto Scharmer

insights.claim: Noema also ran a conversation with complexity scientist Stuart Kauffman titled 'Emergence Is Not Engineering,' part of the same editorial thread questioning whether civilization is at a turning point.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Indicates a cross-disciplinary push (complexity science plus philosophy) to reframe emergent technologies like AI as non-engineerable phenomena, relevant to how 'AI alignment' and 'AI as emergent system' narratives are being shaped in public discourse.
insights.locator: and a conversation with complexity scientist Stuart Kauffman

insights.claim: Philosopher Karl Jaspers described an original Axial Age in which the great religions, philosophies and ethical systems -- China's Confucianism, India's Upanishads and Buddhism, Homer's Greece, and the Hebrew prophets -- emerged in parallel over two millennia ago.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Provides the historical analogy the essay competition (and by extension, Berggruen Institute-aligned thought leadership) is using to argue that today's technological and climate disruptions could similarly reset humanity's foundational belief systems.
insights.quote: the great religions, philosophical outlooks and ethical systems were born around the same time over two millennia ago — China’s Confucianism, India’s Upanishads and Buddhism, Homer’s Greece and the Hebrew prophets.
insights.locator: Karl Jaspers, the German Swiss philosopher

insights.claim: Gardels poses whether today's civilization might again be at a 'hinge of history,' Jaspers's term for a point in time whose events significantly determine the future trajectory of humanity.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Frames the current AI/biotech/climate moment as a potential high-leverage inflection point rather than incremental change -- a lens investors tracking long-duration technology and societal-risk themes may find useful for scenario-planning.
insights.quote: Might our civilization yet again be at a “hinge of history,” as Jaspers described it
insights.locator: Are we poised today to undergo a similar pivotal transformation

insights.claim: Recent advances in genetic engineering, synthetic biology and artificial intelligence are, per Gardels, resurrecting religious and ethical questions about human origins and destiny that had been dormant.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Suggests biotech and AI firms/policymakers should expect renewed public and regulatory scrutiny framed in ethical/existential terms, not just economic or safety terms -- a signal for how AI and biotech regulation narratives may evolve.
insights.locator: Recent leaps in science and technology, notably genetic engineering

insights.claim: The planetary climate crisis is described as putting the survival of the human species itself at risk, adding existential stakes to the argument for a civilizational rethink.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Reinforces that climate risk is being framed by this publication in existential rather than purely economic terms, relevant to how climate-adjacent policy and philanthropic funding narratives (e.g., Berggruen Institute programming) may be positioned.
insights.locator: Even the survival of the species is at risk

insights.claim: With no shared ideational framework and declining trust in inherited faiths and institutions, Gardels argues humanity is being pushed back to first principles, creating an opening for a synchronous global rethink.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: A thesis of institutional-trust erosion driving demand for new unifying frameworks -- relevant background for anyone assessing why AI ethics, techno-philosophy, and civilizational-risk content is gaining an audience right now.
insights.quote: With no shared ideational framework and dwindling trust in bequeathed faiths and institutions, humanity is being forced back to first principles.

insights.claim: The 2026 Berggruen Prize Essay Competition, on the topic 'A New Axial Age?', awards $50,000 for essays submitted in English or Chinese, with winners published and honored at an annual award ceremony.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: A concrete philanthropic/intellectual-capital allocation ($50k, bilingual East-West framing) worth tracking as a barometer of which ideas (here, AI/biotech/climate civilizational risk) elite institutions are willing to fund and amplify.
insights.locator: The competition awards a prize of $50,000

insights.claim: For the 2026 cycle, the Berggruen Prize Essay Competition is, notably, accepting creative fiction submissions in addition to standard essays.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: A format expansion into fiction suggests the sponsoring institution sees speculative/narrative framing as a useful tool for surfacing ideas about AI, biotech and civilizational change that argumentative essays may not capture as well.
insights.locator: For 2026, the competition is accepting creative fiction.

insights.claim: Competition rules bar entrants from using generative AI to create content or substitute original thought, requiring engagement with primary sources; permitted AI use is limited to proofreading, quoting AI output when AI itself is the research subject, and translation -- and any AI use, including AI-assisted translation, must be disclosed on the submission's front page or the entry is disqualified.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: A concrete, enforceable disclosure-based governance model for generative AI in intellectual/creative work -- a template other prizes, journals or institutions assessing AI-in-content-creation policy could adopt or reference.
insights.quote: Entrants must not use generative AI to create content or substitute original thought.
insights.locator: AI Usage: Entrants must not use generative AI

insights.claim: Submissions are capped at 10,000 words in English or 15,000 characters in Chinese, limited to one entry per person per year (co-authorship allowed), due by 11:59 p.m. Pacific Time on Aug. 17, and must be submitted as PDF.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Concrete deadline (Aug. 17) and format constraints for anyone tracking or participating in this thought-leadership channel.
insights.locator: Submission Requirements: All essays must be submitted

insights.claim: Noema's related coverage cited alongside this piece spans Pallavi Aiyar on underlying India-China tensions, Nathan Gardels on Europe's air-conditioning debate amid the climate crisis, and Jacob Dreyer on how AI is rewriting human nature -- showing the publication's concurrent focus on geopolitics, climate and AI as intertwined civilizational themes.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Maps the outlet's current thematic through-line (geopolitics, climate, AI-and-human-nature) that investors monitoring elite-media narrative shifts on these topics may want to follow.
